This adds border-*-radius short hands. For example the new border-top-radius would be a shorthand for border-top-left-radius and border-top-right-radius.

This helps to avoid the awkward current alternative shorthand which is border-radius: 24px 24px 0 0;. It's often difficult for devs to remember the order of corners in the shorthand. And declaring the zeros for corners you don't want to touch seems like extra work we shouldn't really need to do.

Logical equivalence are also included.

Specification title

Support for width and height as css attributes on use element

Specification or proposal URL (if available)

https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG2/struct.html#UseElement

Explainer URL (if available)

No response

Proposal author(s)

No response

MDN URL

No response

Caniuse.com URL

No response

Bugzilla URL

No response

Mozillians who can provide input

No response

WebKit standards-position

No response

Other information

The SVG 2.0 specification introduces support for applying CSS width and height to element, enabling more flexible and consistent styling of reused SVG content. This enhancement allows developers to control element sizing through CSS, improving responsiveness and aligning SVG behavior with modern web styling practices.

With this feature enabled, the following two HTML snippets will now render identically:

Using CSS Properties on the element [1]:

<svg width="100px" height="100px">
 <defs>
    <symbol id="sym" width="80" height="80">
      <rect width="100" height="100" fill="green"/>
    </symbol>
  </defs>
  <use href="#sym" style="width:40px; height:40px"/>
</svg>

Using presentation attributes on the element [2]:

<svg width="100px" height="100px">
 <defs>
    <symbol id="sym" width="80" height="80">
      <rect width="100" height="100" fill="green"/>
    </symbol>
  </defs>
  <use href="#sym" width="40" height="40"/>
</svg>

Note that in Firefox currently the [1] example gives incorrect result, that is, width and height as styles are not applied on use element.
items.title: [SVG] Support for width and height as css attributes on <use> element

No response

No response

Mozillians who can provide input

@emilio

WebKit standards-position

WebKit/standards-positions#519

Other information

Printers usually have a small area at each of the four edges of a sheet of paper that they are not capable of marking reliably, usually due to the printer’s paper handling mechanism. The default page margins are expected to be bigger than these areas, but if authors set margins on their own, and even want to add @page margin boxes (e.g. for custom headers and footers), they need a way of telling where it's safe to print and not.

The CSS environment variable env(safe-printable-inset) can be used to obtain this information. It will be the inset of the largest unprintable area. Although some printers don't have the same unprintable area inset along each of the four paper edges, printers may rotate the print output at their own discretion. The user agent cannot make assumptions about which edge (will it be the long or short edge?) is going to be fed first into the printer. Therefore, only one value can be reliably provided here: The larger of these four values.

Chromestatus entry: https://chromestatus.com/feature/5515971464527872
items.title: Expose unprintable areas via CSS

Other information

There are cases where it's important to distinguish on the server side between cookies that were set by the server and ones that were set by the client.

One such case is cookies that are normally always set by the server, unless some unexpected code (an XSS exploit, a malicious extension, a commit from a confused developer, etc.) happens to set them on the client.

This proposal add a signal that would enable servers to make such a distinction.

httpwg/http-extensions#3110 adds the __Http- prefix.
httpwg/http-extensions#3111 is an ongoing discussion to determine if the combination of the Http and Host prefixes should be __HostHttp- or __Host_Http-.

WebKit standards-position

WebKit/standards-positions#517

Other information

The Web Speech API's contextual biasing functionality allows developers to improve the accuracy of speech recognition by providing a list of specific words or phrases that are likely to be spoken. This is accomplished by creating a SpeechRecognitionPhraseList containing SpeechRecognitionPhrase objects, each with a text string and a numerical "boost" value to indicate how much more likely that phrase is. This enables the speech recognizer to be tailored to the specific context of a web application, such as one containing unique brand names or technical jargon. By giving the recognizer these hints, it is less likely to misinterpret these specific terms, leading to a more accurate and reliable user experience.
items.title: Web Speech API Contextual Biasing

Other information

Short description: #1161 is about pseudo element navigation controls. This property enriches HTML anchor elements functionality to match the pseudo elements one.

Currently to create carousel or table of contents patterns authors can use ::scroll-marker pseudo elements to create navigation elements. As they are pseudo elements they have a number of limitations.

The scroll-target-group property allows to overcome such limitations by making HTML anchor elements 'scroll markers'. By specifying fragment identifier authors have 'scroll target into the view' functionality of ::scroll-markers, but don't have the 'tracking of current scroll marker' one. With scroll-target-group property, browser runs an algorithm to determine the 'current scroll marker' and authors can style such anchor element with :target-current pseudo class.
items.title: CSS scroll-target-group property
